subject: Frontier estimation using a quadratic function.

messages.author: 0bfa94c1afe543dd
messages.subject: Frontier estimation using a quadratic function.
parts:
Hi, 

I have a quick question about the model I've been working on lately. I've tried to do a basic frontier estimation of a scatter plot. I set up a quadratic function of ax^2 + bx + c to be a frontier and want to estimate three parameters a,b, and c. I make an arbitrary likelihood function that assigns the probability of 0.1 to data points below this frontier and very low probability like \exp(-100) to points outside the frontier. My only prior knowledge is that a is between -1 and 0 and b is negative and c is gamma (2,2). I would expect that posterior of a,b and c are estimated so that the frontier covers almost all data points. However, the quadratic function with the estimated parameters only covers some part of data points, at most a half of them. I suspect that I made a mistake coding this model up in stan. Could you take a look at if the following code makes sense? Any comments will be appreciated! 

functions{
  real distance_log(real y, real x, real a, real b, real c){
    real k;
    k<- if_else(y < a*x^2 + b*x +c, 0.1,exp(-10));
    return log(k);
  }
}
data{
  int<lower=0> N;
  real y[N];
  real x[N];
}
parameters{
  real<lower=-1,upper=0> a;
  real<upper=0> b;
  real c;
}
model{
  c~gamma(2,2);
  for(i in 1:N){
    increment_log_prob(distance_log(y[i],x[i],a,b,c));
  }
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Frontier estimation using a quadratic function.
parts:
Stan isn't really intended for this kind of problem --- it's for
sampling or optimizing continuous densities. I'm not
sure you have a proper posterior given the constraints and
gamma prior.

One thing you could try doing is have the probability drop off if
the boundary's far away and have that dropoff be asymmetric above
and below. I think it might work to have a half normal above
with a large scale and a half normal below with a small scale.

I'm also not sure what you mean by the frontier covering all the
data points.

The way to write your function would've returned log(0.1) and -10
rather than going the exp and log round trip --- but you need to
replace this for use in Stan, so it's a moot point.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Frontier estimation using a quadratic function.
parts:
Identifying three parameters of a quadratic function is no problem.
That's just a regression. For that, all you need to do is declare
x and y as vectors, a, b, and c as scalar (real) parameters,
sigma as a positive-constrained parameter, and do this:

y ~ normal(a + b * x + c * x^2, sigma);

That then gives you a quadratic with symmetric normal noise scaled
as sigma.

But what you seem to want to do is solve an optimization
problem with a data-driven constraint. So you seem to want the noise
to be asymmetric above and below the estimated value. There's not
a neat way to do this that requires the noise to be positive (that is,
the curve picked out by a, b, and c to produce values for x below
observed values for y [or vice-versa]) that I can see in Stan.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Frontier estimation using a quadratic function.
parts:
This can be framed as a form of density estimation —
essentially the data are drawn uniform from below the
quadratic and exponential above it. What you have to
be careful with are the normalizations — you can’t just
define a “distance function” you have to define a well-posed
probability density over probability densities (i.e. over the
parameter {a, b, c} which define probability densities over
the data).

Once you’ve done that you can run Stan to get a posterior
distribution over these probability densities.

messages.author: 0bfa94c1afe543dd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Frontier estimation using a quadratic function.
parts: Thanks Bob and Mike. Following your advice, I discarded my "distance function" and did a simple regression using the normal distribution. Instead of setting the noise to be asymmetric, I introduced an additional function \exp(-u) by which the predictor is multiplied. In this model, u is skewed normal truncated at zero, so the estimated quadratic curve is above data points (but not all data points due to the stochastic property coming from tau). The following is the code. Even though sampling is really slow, the result is quite satisfactory. Thanks again for your advice and I'd appreciate any further comments on this code. Thanks you!

data{
  int<lower=0> N;
  real y[N];
  real x[N];
}
parameters{

real<upper=0> a;
  real<upper=0> b;
  real<lower=0> c;
  real<lower=0> u;
  real<lower=0> tau;
  real<lower=0> eta;
}
model{
  c~normal(8,0.5);
  u~skew_normal(2,1,eta);
  eta~normal(2,0.5);
  tau~normal(0,0.5);

  for(i in 1:N){
  real z[N];
  z[i]<-a*square(x[i])+b*x[i]+c;
increment_log_prob(normal_log(y[i],z[i]*exp(-u),tau));

}
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Frontier estimation using a quadratic function.
parts:
> On Oct 18, 2015, at 3:25 PM, Jangho Yang <yangj...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Bob and Mike. Following your advice, I discarded my "distance function" and did a simple regression using the normal distribution. Instead of setting the noise to be asymmetric, I introduced an additional function \exp(-u) by which the predictor is multiplied. In this model, u is skewed normal truncated at zero, so the estimated quadratic curve is above data points (but not all data points due to the stochastic property coming from tau). The following is the code. Even though sampling is really slow, the result is quite satisfactory. Thanks again for your advice and I'd appreciate any further comments on this code. Thanks you!
>
> data{
> int<lower=0> N;
> real y[N];
> real x[N];
> }
> parameters{
> real<upper=0> a;
> real<upper=0> b;
> real<lower=0> c;
> real<lower=0> u;
> real<lower=0> tau;
> real<lower=0> eta;
> }
> model{
> c~normal(8,0.5);
> u~skew_normal(2,1,eta);
> eta~normal(2,0.5);
> tau~normal(0,0.5);
>
> for(i in 1:N){
> real z[N];
> z[i]<-a*square(x[i])+b*x[i]+c;
> increment_log_prob(normal_log(y[i],z[i]*exp(-u),tau));

If you declare x as a vectors, you can replace the
for loop with a vectorized version:

y ~ normal(exp(-u) * (a * (x .* x) + b * x + c), tau);

Each iteration should run faster.

- Bob
